snippets: <jats:p>This paper studies the impact of the order of senders in the sequential Bayesian persuasion game on the receiver's equilibrium utility. We find that it is always optimal for the receiver to put the more aligned sender before the less aligned sender. Comparative statics analysis shows that when we restrict to senders who are alignable, as the degree of misalignment between senders increases or as the number of senders increases, the receiver's equilibrium utility may decrease. In addition, we find that when senders are alignable, the sequential game performs no worse than the simultaneous game in terms of information disclosure.</jats:p>

snippets: <jats:p>This paper argues that crises do not destroy governmental rationality; they reveal what has always existed beneath the surface. I introduce a behavioral–institutional framework showing that governments systematically fall into what can be called the “Survival–Rationality Gap”: a state in which policymakers know the correct economic action but are incentivized to choose the politically safer but economically inferior option. Using behavioral bias, institutional constraints, and expectation shocks—supported by a micro‑level managerial case—the paper suggests that suboptimal policymaking is often not a “bad choice” but a “survival‑optimized choice.” The paper concludes by asking whether crisis‑resilient policymaking requires institutional redesign or a redefinition of political survival itself.</jats:p>
